title: Multi-GPU serving design: tensor & pipeline parallelism, NCCL tuning, sharding
content:
Context and purpose:
This doc collects design decisions, trade-offs, and a short experimental plan for Multi-GPU model serving in the Redwood runtime. Target audience: serving runtime engineers, applied ML, SRE, and release engineering. The goal is to provide a single-reference design for enabling models that exceed a single GPU (memory or perf) via tensor/pipeline parallelism, efficient NCCL-based communication, and pragmatic sharding of model state and KV cache.

Goals / non-goals:
- Goals:
  - Support production-serving for models that require >1 GPU (parameter or activation partitioning) with predictable latency and throughput.
  - Minimize cross-GPU synchronization overhead for common inference workloads (short sequences, streaming).
  - Provide configuration knobs and safe fallbacks (replicated vs sharded) to trade cost vs latency.
- Non-goals:
  - This doc does not fully design training-time pipeline parallelism semantics; focus is inference-serving patterns and optimizations.

High-level approaches considered:
1) Tensor parallelism (TP): split large weight matrices across devices and run fused kernels with collective ops. Good when model compute per token is high and the communication volume (all-reduce or reduce-scatter + all-gather) is manageable relative to compute.
2) Pipeline parallelism (PP): split transformer layers across stages/GPUs and stream micro-batches through the pipeline. Helpful to increase GPU utilization and support very large models by trading added pipeline latency.
3) Hybrid TP+PP: combine TP within a stage and PP across stages for very large models. More complex orchestration but required for largest models.
4) Model sharding: sharding parameters/optimizer (for inference only parameters) across GPUs to reduce memory footprint; for inference we focus on parameter sharding and KV cache sharding.

Design constraints from serving use-cases:
- Low tail latency (p50/p90 targets per deployment tier) is critical; we must avoid large synchronization barriers on the critical path.
- Many small requests with short sequences (<= 128 tokens) dominate hosted traffic; batching windows should be short and preemptible.
- Streaming & early token return are supported; cannot block generation behind full micro-batch completion if using PP.
- Customers expect deterministic fallbacks when a multi-GPU node loses a GPU: ability to degrade to fewer GPUs or fallback to a smaller replicated model.

Architecture proposal (core components):
- Stage manager: per-node orchestration that maps logical model stages (PP) and tensor shards (TP) onto physical GPUs, plus lifecycle (startup, migrate, drain).
- Communication layer: NCCL-backed transport for collective ops, with pluggable fallback to socket-based RPC for environments without RDMA.
- KV cache store: hybrid local + sharded global view. Each GPU owns the KV shards for tokens it computed; lightweight index maps route attention queries to the right shard. Cross-GPU reads are served via direct P2P or collectives depending on access pattern.
- Scheduler: continuous batching engine that groups incoming requests into micro-batches per model-version+replica; aware of PP pipeline stage boundaries and KPIs (latency SLO, cost target).
- Kernel layer: fused attention and MLP kernels that can operate on sharded tensors (reduce-scatter/all-gather friendly) and expose workspace hooks for fused quantized kernels.

Tensor vs Pipeline decisions (when to use which):
- Use TP when: model large but fits in memory across TP group without requiring extra pipeline stages; latency sensitive workloads where pipeline fill/drain cost would hurt short sequences.
- Use PP when: model has too many layers to fit in TP only, or when per-GPU memory for activations is the bottleneck. PP helps reduce peak memory by splitting layers.
- Hybrid: for very large models (e.g., billions of params) use 2-4-way TP inside each PP stage.

NCCL and cross-GPU comms (practical guidance):
- Leverage NCCL collectives for bandwidth-efficient all-reduce/all-gather/reduce-scatter. Benchmark nccl-tests on target hardware to select topology and IB settings.
- Provide fallback non-NCCL implementations (gRPC/UCX or socket) for private/offline environments that lack tuned RDMA.
- Tunables to surface in the console/config: NCCL algorithm preference (ring vs tree), fusion thresholds (message sizes), P2P vs host-mediated transfers, and whether to prefer intra-node SHM.
- Diagnostic knobs: NCCL_DEBUG=INFO, run nccl-tests to validate latency vs bandwidth, and track per-collective latency in traces.
- Practical tips observed in experiments:
  - For small messages (few KB), the overhead of collectives is non-trivial; prefer P2P or aggregated gather strategies to reduce the number of collectives.
  - For large tensors (10s–100s MB), all-reduce / reduce-scatter scales well.

KV cache design (inference-specific):
Requirements:
- Must support prefix caching across steps for streaming generation.
- Efficient per-request access when cache is sharded across GPUs.
- Minimal synchronization to append new tokens and read keys/values for next-token computation.

Options considered:
A) Replicated KV on each GPU: simplest, low-latency local reads at the cost of memory duplication. Good for small models or when per-GPU memory budget allows.
B) Sharded KV per-attention head/sequence chunk: distribute KV across GPUs to save memory. Reads require cross-GPU reads/collectives or staged streaming.
C) Hybrid: replicate recent tokens (last N timesteps) locally and shard older tokens. This reduces cross-GPU reads for streaming sessions.

Recommended approach (initial implementation):
- Default to replicated KV for hosted-small instances (latency-focused).
- For dedicated/large models, implement sharded KV where each GPU stores KV for a slice of the sequence range (e.g., round-robin or contiguous ranges). Use asynchronous prefetch for upcoming reads and combine with intra-step reduce-scatter for attention scoring to reduce blocking.
- Provide tooling to choose the policy per-deployment: policy = replicated | sharded | hybrid; expose heuristics: if model_params > X and active_seq_mem > Y => sharded.

Scheduling and batching across stages:
- Continuous batching: aggregator accepts requests and forms micro-batches with a small max_wait (e.g., 5–10ms) and a max_batch_size bound. Micro-batches should be labeled with stage IDs so pipeline stages can accept them and forward without global barriers.
- Pipeline micro-batching: adopt a multi-queue approach where each stage has an input queue; backpressure signals propagate to earlier stages when queues saturate.
- Preemption: allow high-priority requests to preempt batch slots by stealing unused capacity or by being injected as single-item micro-batches that bypass batching for latency-sensitive flows.
- KV-aware scheduling: when KV is sharded, prefer to schedule requests such that their required KV shards are co-located or already cached on the target GPUs to minimize cross-GPU reads. This may require sticky routing or short-lived affinity.

Kernel considerations and optimizations:
- Implement fused attention kernels that accept sharded inputs and produce sharded outputs with a single fused collective (reduce-scatter + local compute + all-gather).
- Support quantized kernels (int8/fp8) where applicable; provide a path to verify quality regressions via eval harness. Quantized kernels may change communication patterns (smaller messages).
- Memory layout: prefer blocked layouts matching cuBLAS/cuDNN expectations and reduce copies between collectives. Reserve a reusable workspace per GPU to avoid repeated allocations.

Fallbacks and graceful degradation:
- Replica fallback: when a GPU fails or network partition occurs, degrade to fewer GPUs by shifting to a replicated smaller model variant (if available) or by failing-over to a host that runs a replicated single-GPU variant.
- Canary and rollout: test multi-GPU configurations in shadow mode with mirrored traffic and compare p50/p90 and correctness before promoting to production.

Metrics and observability to collect:
- Per-stage per-collective latency and throughput (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter).
- KV cache hit/miss rates, cross-GPU read latency, and bytes transferred per inference.
- Scheduler metrics: batch sizes, wait times, preemptions, and queue lengths.
- System metrics: GPU utilization, PCIe/NIC utilization, memory fragmentation.

Experiment plan / benchmarks:
- Baseline: single-GPU replicated model for small model family. Measure p50/p90/p99 and cost per token.
- TP-only: run 2-way/4-way TP for medium models; measure collective overhead and token latency.
- PP-only: run 2-stage PP with varying micro-batch sizes to quantify pipeline fill/drain overhead for typical short sequences.
- Hybrid: run TP+PP for largest models. Evaluate per-token latency and throughput vs cost.
- KV policies: compare replicated vs sharded vs hybrid on memory footprint and latency.
- NCCL tuning sweep: nccl-tests for ring/tree variants, measure small-message and large-message performance across network fabrics.

Open questions / trade-offs:
- How aggressive should default sharding heuristics be? (Memory savings vs increased tail latency.)
- What affinity policies are acceptable for multi-tenant hosted infra? Sticky routing can improve performance but may reduce packing efficiency.
- How to expose safety knobs to customers vs keep defaults tuned for low latency?

Next steps / action items:
- Build a small prototype for TP-only (2-way) on a multi-GPU node and collect nccl-tests + real-workload traces (owner: Ethan Chen, due: 2024-06-16).
- Implement basic KV sharding prototype with hybrid replication of recent tokens (owner: Priya Nair, due: 2024-06-30).
- Integrate per-collective tracing into Redwood console and add dashboards for all-reduce/all-gather latencies (owner: Liam O'Connor, due: 2024-07-15).
- Draft canary plan and gating metrics for rollout to hosted API (owner: Sofia Ramirez, due: 2024-07-01).

References and artifacts:
- Linked artifacts in metadata above; see github:redwood/realtime-inference#768 for early prototype code.
- Benchmarks and nccl-tests outputs are stored in doc:multi-gpu-benchmarks-2024.

Notes / rough meeting log (working):
- 2024-05-03: discussed trade-offs between sticky affinity and packing efficiency — leaning toward default no-affinity but sticky for large (>64k token-hour) sessions.
- 2024-05-17: prototype results showed reduce-scatter+local-compute+all-gather pattern reduces peak PCIe pressure vs naive all-gather per-layer.

This is a working doc; expect follow-ups and more concrete microbenchmarks in separate artifacts.
